page: Microsoft Azure D96lds_v7 is a compute-optimized virtual machine from the Dldsv7 family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 96 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 48 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor operating at 4.2 GHz. The system is equipped with 192.0 GB of system memory, yielding a resource density of 2.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It includes 5669 GB of local storage and supports Premium Storage, but does not bundle any GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

The underlying x86_64 architecture supports advanced instruction sets, including Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX-512) and Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX). In performance testing, the server demonstrates top-tier multi-threaded capabilities, scoring 108246.31 on the PassMark CPU test and achieving a top-tier rating in extended instructions. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression reaches 611.35 GB/sec, while stress-ng multi-core performance is rated as strong. Single-core performance is more moderate, with stress-ng single-core scoring in the average tier.

Memory performance is highly competitive, with small-block cached read bandwidth reaching a top-tier speed of 7403.16 GB/sec, and large-block read/write bandwidths remaining strong. The server excels in database and web serving workloads, delivering 159.81 million operations per second in Redis SET benchmarks and 150.35 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. Large language model (LLM) prompt processing is exceptionally fast, scoring in the top tier across small, medium, and large models, though text generation speeds drop to average for large models.

Given its 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, the D96lds_v7 is optimized for compute-heavy tasks rather than memory-intensive databases. However, the inclusion of 5669 GB of local storage and top-tier database operation benchmarks makes it highly suitable for high-throughput web serving, LLM prompt processing, multi-threaded data compression, and compute-bound database operations where massive RAM capacity is not the primary constraint.
